clinicalPearls: Caused by variants in KCNMA1, which encodes the pore-forming alpha subunit of the large-conductance calcium- and voltage-activated potassium (BK, Slo1) channel that couples intracellular calcium to potassium efflux and shapes the afterhyperpolarisation
The phenotype combines epilepsy, a paroxysmal movement disorder, and variable developmental impairment, with considerable overlap between features
A characteristic presentation is paroxysmal non-kinesigenic dyskinesia, sometimes co-occurring with generalised epilepsy in the same individual or family

Gain-of-function variants tend to associate with paroxysmal dyskinesia and absence-type epilepsy, whereas loss-of-function variants more often cause developmental delay, ataxia, and structural or movement abnormalities
Seizure types include absence, generalised tonic-clonic, and other generalised or focal seizures depending on the variant
Distinguishing gain from loss of function is therapeutically relevant, as the two ends of the spectrum behave differently
Cerebellar signs, ataxia, and cognitive impairment can feature at the loss-of-function end
reference.pathophysiology: KCNMA1 encodes the alpha subunit of the BK channel (Slo1), a large-conductance potassium channel activated jointly by membrane depolarisation and rising intracellular calcium. By linking calcium entry to rapid potassium efflux, BK channels sharpen action potentials, drive the fast afterhyperpolarisation, and regulate neurotransmitter release and neuronal and smooth-muscle excitability. Gain-of-function variants increase potassium current and can produce paroxysmal dyskinesia and absence epilepsy through altered firing dynamics, whereas loss-of-function variants reduce the current and are associated with developmental delay, ataxia, and cerebellar involvement. The dual calcium and voltage sensitivity of the channel explains why disturbances manifest as paroxysmal movement and seizure phenomena.
additionalDifferentials: GLUT1 deficiency with paroxysmal movement and epilepsy
Genetic generalised epilepsies with absence seizures
additionalInvestigations: Gene panel or whole-exome sequencing to identify the KCNMA1 variant
Electroencephalography to characterise absence or other seizure types
Brain magnetic resonance imaging, particularly to assess for cerebellar or structural changes
Video documentation of paroxysmal dyskinetic episodes and their triggers
Functional characterisation to distinguish gain from loss of function where available
redFlags: Frequent or prolonged paroxysmal dyskinetic attacks impairing function
Status epilepticus or escalating seizure frequency
Falls or injury from paroxysmal episodes
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the variant and phenotype: gain-of-function paroxysmal dyskinesia with absence epilepsy may have relatively preserved cognition, while loss-of-function disease with developmental delay and ataxia typically carries greater long-term impairment.
pitfalls: Treating the paroxysmal dyskinesia as psychogenic rather than a channelopathy
Assuming a single functional mechanism when gain and loss of function diverge clinically
Overlooking the co-occurrence of movement disorder and epilepsy in the same patient
Missing cerebellar signs at the loss-of-function end
